title: A map projection is a rule for laying a round Earth on a flat sheet
body:
## What the manual is

The U.S. Geological Survey Publications Warehouse lists John P. Snyder, *Map projections: A working manual*, Professional Paper 1395, 1987, at the URL above. That manual is the working reference this card points to for constructing and comparing projections.

A projection is a systematic rule that assigns coordinates on a plane to locations on the Earth. The Earth parameters that enter the rule — an equatorial radius, a polar radius, a chosen meridian — are measurements and conventions, documented on the shape and prime-meridian cards. The projection is the next step: which of those locations go where on the paper.

## What has to give

A flattened orange peel tears or stretches. That is the geometric constraint. No rule can send every point of a spheroid to a plane and keep all of area, shape, distance, and direction at once. Different projections keep different subsets of those properties, which is why a working manual compares them instead of crowning one map. Snyder's book is cited as that manual. Particular scale-factor formulas were not re-read from the PDF, so none are printed here.

**Fact:** the 1987 USGS manual exists and is the professional reference for this job, and a projection is a chosen rule with chosen distortions.

**Interpretation:** a world map that looks "obvious" is still a rule. The Mercator projection, for example, is one rule among those the manual treats. Calling a familiar wall map the shape of the world confuses the rule with the planet.
